opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really impressive achievement, and I don't want to downplay it. When a model can take a hard open problem and produce a correct proof, that's remarkable engineering. But I think we're conflating two different things: answering a question and asking a new one.

Most of the proofs we're seeing are for problems that humans already framed. Someone decades ago looked at the landscape of mathematics and said, "Here's a conjecture worth caring about." The hard creative act was often that framing step. Then the proof is a kind of very sophisticated search: you know where the target is, and you need to find a path to it. Models are getting very good at that search, partly because they've absorbed an enormous amount of the existing toolkit.

If you look at what we usually call scientific breakthroughs, Copernicus, Darwin, Einstein, even something like the invention of category theory, they weren't someone efficiently filling in the next box on a list. They were someone saying the list itself is wrong, or the question we've all been asking is the wrong question. That's often counter to the consensus of the training data. A breakthrough is frequently the thing that looks like a mistake from inside the existing paradigm.

That's my worry about how we build these systems. We're training them to be extremely good students, the A+ student who knows every textbook and can answer any exam question. But the people who change a field aren't always the best exam takers. They're the ones willing to be wrong in an interesting direction, to challenge an assumption everyone else treats as given.

So what I'd call a real breakthrough from AI isn't "it solved conjecture X." It's "it proposed a new conjecture, or a new framework, that surprised experts and that turned out to be fruitful." We don't have benchmarks for that, and that's partly the problem. We measure what's easy to measure, which is answering known questions, and then we declare we've automated science. I think we've automated a very important part of it, but not the part that's historically produced the big jumps.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts proving problems humans have already framed with the creative act of posing a new question.

r002.rationale: It presents reframing questions and proposing fruitful new conjectures or frameworks as what drives major breakthroughs and changes fields.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, and I want to be careful here because I don't want to dismiss what these models are doing. Solving an IMO problem, or proving a theorem that's been open for a while, that's genuinely impressive. But I think when people see that and say "look, AI is doing science now," they're confusing two very different things.

A proof is the answer to a question somebody already asked. The question is well-posed, you know what success looks like, and there's a verifier at the end. That's a search problem. It can be an incredibly hard search problem, and the models are getting very good at it, but structurally it's the same kind of thing as playing Go very well.

What actually makes a breakthrough in science is almost never the answer. It's the question. If you look at Copernicus, or Einstein, or the people who figured out the structure of DNA, the hard part was not computing something. The hard part was noticing that everyone around them was asking the wrong question, or had a framing that was slightly off, and being stubborn enough to say "no, I think the interesting thing is over here." And at the moment they did that, there was no benchmark telling them they were right. Most of their peers thought they were wasting their time.

So the thing I worry about is that we've built these systems to be, essentially, very very good students. They've read everything, they're agreeable, they want to give you the answer you're looking for. And a very good student is not the same thing as a scientist. In fact, a lot of the best scientists were kind of bad students. They were contrarian. They were comfortable sitting with something that didn't make sense for years.

Our training objective pushes almost the opposite way. We reward the model for being right according to what we already know. We don't really have a way to reward it for being interestingly wrong, or for picking a direction that only pays off a decade later. And so you get this situation where the models can fill in the frontier very efficiently, they can close gaps, they can do the kind of work that a strong postdoc does. That's valuable, I'm not knocking it. But that's not the same as moving the frontier.

So when I see a headline that says an AI produced a new proof, my reaction is: okay, who asked the question? If a human posed it, then the human did the part that's actually rare. The model did the part that's actually hard, but hard and rare aren't the same thing.

r001.rationale: It contrasts solving a question someone has already posed, with a verifier for success, against identifying the question or reframing the problem.

r002.rationale: It says that questions and reframing drive scientific breakthroughs, but does not identify questions that open new fields of research as the central contribution.

astra-6.text:
I think it confuses finding an answer with finding the question. A mathematical proof can absolutely be new mathematics, and an AI producing one can be a significant achievement. But if we give the system a conjecture and ask it to prove it, we’ve already supplied a lot of the intellectual framing: what matters, what the objects are, what success looks like.

The part that interests me is whether a system can challenge that framing. Can it notice something everyone else has overlooked, introduce a useful new concept, or ask a question we didn’t know we should ask? Scientific breakthroughs often change our understanding of which problems are worth solving.

So I wouldn’t dismiss AI-generated proofs. I’d just be careful about what we infer from them. Being very good at solving problems we can already state is evidence of a powerful capability. It doesn’t, by itself, establish the ability to open up a new scientific direction.

r001.rationale: It contrasts proving a supplied conjecture with challenging the framing and identifying problems worth solving.

r002.rationale: It says breakthroughs can change which problems are worth solving and highlights asking questions we did not know to ask as opening a new scientific direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it confuses finding an answer with changing the way we think about a problem. A mathematical proof can absolutely be a scientific breakthrough. But the fact that an AI produces a new proof doesn’t, by itself, tell us how significant that advance is.

When we evaluate these systems, we typically give them a question that humans have already formulated. We’ve chosen the objects, defined the problem, and decided that solving it would be interesting. That’s a substantial amount of intellectual work before the model even starts.

What I’m interested in is whether a system can challenge that framing. Can it notice that we’re asking the wrong question? Can it introduce a concept that makes a whole set of problems understandable in a different way? A proof might do exactly that, but you have to look at what it contributes, rather than simply whether it’s new and correct.

So I wouldn’t dismiss AI-generated proofs. I would distinguish success on a problem we’ve supplied from the ability to open up a new direction of inquiry. Both matter, but they’re different capabilities.

r001.rationale: It contrasts solving a question humans supplied with challenging the framing, noticing the wrong question, and opening a new direction of inquiry.

r002.rationale: It mentions opening a new direction of inquiry, but does not clearly say that asking questions that open new fields is central to major scientific breakthroughs.
